issues.legal_issue: Dying declarations are unsafe to rely on when the declarants sustained injuries likely to impair their brain functions.
material_facts: Both declarants had deep incised wounds that penetrated the brain, with brain tissue protruding from the wounds.
A doctor recorded the statements after the injuries were sustained.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified in declining to rely on the dying declarations because the brain injuries made it extremely unsafe to place credence on the statements.
issues.legal_principle: A dying declaration should not be relied on where the declarant’s injuries are such that the declarant’s brain functions would likely have been impaired.

predicates.criminal_case: The proceeding concerned a criminal prosecution based on alleged fatal assaults.
predicates.declarants_sustained_brain_deep_injuries: The declarants sustained wounds that penetrated the brain.

issues.definition: When a criminal case relies on declarations by people who sustained brain-deep injuries, the declarations are unsafe to rely on.

issues.legal_issue: Eyewitness testimony should not be rejected merely because the witnesses are related to the victims, independent witnesses were not called, or witnesses differ about which nearby exit the assailants used.
material_facts: Several witnesses living nearby heard cries during the night, rushed to the scene, and testified that they saw the assailants fleeing, including some carrying axes.
The witnesses were relatives of the victims, and no independent witness was called.
Some witnesses differed about whether the assailants left through the eastern or western gate of the same house.
The record did not establish that an independent person who had witnessed a relevant event was left uncalled.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in rejecting the eyewitness evidence on these grounds; the discrepancy about the gate was not a material contradiction, and the witnesses’ relationship to the victims did not by itself justify rejecting their testimony.
issues.legal_principle: The natural witnesses to an incident at a dwelling may be its inmates or nearby residents, and courts should not insist on unrelated witnesses who may not have seen the event. Non-examination of an independent witness warrants adverse comment where the evidence or investigation records disclose that such a person witnessed a relevant event. Discrepancies should be assessed in light of the core evidence and broad probabilities, including the circumstances in which witnesses observed events.

predicates.witnesses_saw_assailants_flee: The witnesses testified that they saw the assailants leaving the scene.

predicates.discrepancy_concerned_nearby_exits: Witnesses differed about which of two nearby exits the assailants used.

issues.definition: Where witnesses respond to cries, see assailants flee, and differ only about nearby exits, their testimony is not discarded merely because they are related or no independent eyewitness is shown to have been left uncalled.

issues.legal_issue: Failure to determine the origin of blood on a recovered weapon does not eliminate the weapon’s circumstantial evidentiary value when the failure may result from disintegration of the blood.
material_facts: Two axes were recovered after the accused gave information that they had concealed them.
Blood was detected on both axes; the blood on one was found to be human, while the origin of the blood on the other could not be determined because it had disintegrated.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in substantially discounting the recovery evidence because the origin of the blood on one axe could not be determined; the recovery remained a circumstance for consideration.
issues.legal_principle: A failure to identify the origin of blood because a stain is insufficient or has undergone hematological changes does not establish that it was not human blood and does not invariably deprive recovery evidence of value. Prabhu Babaji v. State of Bombay, AIR 1956 SC 51, and Raghav Prapanna Tripathi v. State of U.P., AIR 1963 SC 74, were decided on materially different facts and do not establish such a categorical rule. A court should assess the circumstance objectively rather than entertain imaginative doubts.

predicates.accused_concealed_weapons_recovered_on_i: Weapons were recovered from places where the accused said they had concealed them.

issues.definition: When accused persons’ information leads to recovery of concealed weapons bearing blood, the recovery retains circumstantial weight even if the blood’s origin cannot be determined because it disintegrated.

issues.legal_issue: Obtaining an accused person’s signature on a recovery memorandum does not invalidate recovery evidence relating to a fact discovered under Section 27 of the Evidence Act.
material_facts: The investigating officer obtained the accused persons’ signatures on memoranda recording recoveries of axes made following information given by them.
The recoveries concerned weapons that the accused had said they had concealed.
issues.conclusion: The signatures did not vitiate the recovery evidence: Section 162(1) of the Code did not apply to statements falling within Section 27 of the Evidence Act, and obtaining the signatures was not itself illegal.
issues.legal_principle: Section 162(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure prohibits signing a statement made to a police officer during investigation, but Section 162(2) preserves the operation of Section 27 of the Evidence Act. An investigating officer need not obtain an accused’s signature on a statement concerning a recovery under Section 27; obtaining it does not, by itself, make the recovery evidence illegal or vitiated. The Court relied on Tahsildar Singh v. State of U.P., AIR 1959 SC 1012, and Razik Ram v. J.S. Chouhan, AIR 1975 SC 667, regarding the purpose of Section 162.

issues.legal_issue: A party may seek to recall a witness for further cross-examination when a prior inconsistent statement becomes available later in the proceedings, and the earlier statement is not unavailable merely because the witness was examined before the inconsistency emerged.
material_facts: A police witness initially testified that the informant had not named the assailants, but later, when cross-examined by the prosecutor, accepted that he had told the investigating officer the informant had named them.
The informant was examined later, but the defence did not ask him whether he had named the assailants to the police witness.

The Court noted that the defence could have sought recall for further cross-examination and declined to provide a further opportunity after the informant retraced his earlier position in cross-examination.
issues.conclusion: The alleged prior statement was available for use to challenge the witness’s credibility through recall and further cross-examination; the Court did not accept that it was unavailable and declined to grant a further opportunity in the circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: Section 155(3) of the Evidence Act permits impeachment of a witness’s credit by proof of a former statement inconsistent with testimony, and the judgment identifies Section 14 as prescribing the mode of using such a statement for contradiction. A party may seek recall for further cross-examination when the relevant statement emerges later. The Court relied on Naba Kumar Das v. Rudra Narayan Jana, AIR 1923 PC 95.

predicates.criminal_case: The proceeding concerned a criminal prosecution based on alleged fatal assaults.
predicates.prior_inconsistent_statement_emerged_lat: A statement bearing on a witness’s credibility became apparent after the relevant witness had been examined.
predicates.party_did_not_seek_recall_to_confront_wi: The party did not seek to recall the witness for further cross-examination about the later-emerging statement.

issues.definition: When a prior inconsistent statement emerges later in a criminal case, it remains available for impeachment through recall even if the party did not seek recall to confront the witness.

issues.legal_issue: An acquittal must be set aside and the trial conviction restored when the cumulative circumstances against particular accused persons establish that they were the assailants.
material_facts: The prosecution appeal challenged an acquittal that had reversed trial convictions.
There was undisputed evidence of hostility arising from property disputes and proceedings initiated against two accused persons.
Witnesses testified that they saw those two accused among the assailants fleeing the scene with axes.
Axes were recovered after information from those two accused, and blood was found on both, with human origin established for the blood on one.
The Court considered the circumstances against those two accused sturdy in combination and found their cumulative effect irresistible; the remaining respondents were not included in that conclusion.
issues.conclusion: The Court set aside the acquittal of the two accused against whom the cumulative circumstances were established and restored their trial convictions and sentences.
issues.legal_principle: The circumstances against an accused must be evaluated cumulatively. Motive may be considered alongside eyewitness evidence and recovery evidence; where their combined effect establishes guilt, an acquittal cannot stand. The Court applied this principle to the appeal against acquittal and restored the trial court’s convictions for the two accused concerned.
